title: Mac's Mom Burns Her House Down

jokes.text: Charles Grodin is coming in concert, and you didn't tell us?
jokes.setup: Dee mentions Josh Groban, a famous singer, with excitement
jokes.punchline: Mac and Charlie mishear/misremember it as Charles Grodin, the famously grumpy actor, and are enthusiastic about seeing HIM in concert
jokes.explanation: The joke works on multiple levels: Mac and Charlie's idiocy is perfectly calibrated — they don't just mishear, they're ENTHUSIASTIC about Charles Grodin in concert, which is a wonderfully specific choice. Grodin as a beloved figure to these dumb guys adds texture. Well-structured misdirection.

jokes.text: He brings out the curmudgeon in me.
jokes.setup: Mac and Charlie are enthusiastically defending Charles Grodin as a performer they love
jokes.punchline: Mac's reason for loving him is that Grodin 'brings out the curmudgeon' in him — an absurdly self-aware and pretentious thing for Mac to say
jokes.explanation: Perfect economy — five words that reveal Mac's delusional self-image. Mac is himself a curmudgeon but would never see it that way; he thinks Grodin UNLOCKS something in him. The line is quotable and character-specific.

dialogue.speaker: Mac
dialogue.line: Call Charles Grodin a bitter old man one more time and see what happens!

jokes.text: Josh Groban. Oh. Is he Charles Grodin's son?
jokes.setup: Dee corrects them that it's Josh Groban, not Charles Grodin
jokes.punchline: Charlie's response isn't embarrassment but doubling down — speculating that Groban must be Grodin's son, thus preserving their enthusiasm
jokes.explanation: This escalates the previous joke beautifully. Charlie's logic — that Groban must be Grodin's son, so he's 'probably funny' — is exactly how these characters think. It extends the bit without losing steam and shows the characters' unshakeable commitment to wrong beliefs. The 'He's probably funny' follow-up seals it.

dialogue.speaker: Mac
dialogue.line: They're not terrorists! They're just Muslims.

jokes.text: If he's related to Charles Grodin, he is. Don't worry about that.
jokes.setup: Charlie speculates that Josh Groban might be funny if he's Charles Grodin's son
jokes.punchline: Mac confidently endorses this wrong logic as settled fact
jokes.explanation: A solid button on the Grodin/Groban bit. Mac's authoritative endorsement of incorrect information is classic character work, though it's a third beat on the same joke and starts to diminish returns.

dialogue.speaker: Dennis
dialogue.line: I'm very much looking forward to not taking care of anyone when I'm older.

jokes.text: Call Charles Grodin a bitter old man one more time, and see what happens!
jokes.setup: Dee accurately describes Charles Grodin as 'a bitter old man with a giant head' versus Josh Groban as a beautiful singer
jokes.punchline: Mac takes this as a personal affront and threatens Dee on behalf of Charles Grodin
jokes.explanation: The perfect cap to the Grodin bit. Mac's protective rage on behalf of Charles Grodin — a stranger he has never met — is completely unhinged and perfectly in character. 'See what happens!' delivers the threat with genuine menace, which makes it funnier. Highly quotable and a strong closer to the cold open's A-joke.

dialogue.speaker: Dennis
dialogue.line: Hell, no, I'm not going to take care of you; you were a terrible father to me.

jokes.text: Mac's phone call: 'No, they're not terrorists! They're just Muslims.' / 'Okay, well, I'm gonna hang up, okay? Hanging up.'
jokes.setup: Mac is trying to leave the bar and gets a phone call from his mom mid-conversation
jokes.punchline: His mom is apparently reporting the neighbors as terrorists; Mac's correction 'They're just Muslims' treats casual Islamophobia as a reasonable de-escalation, then he immediately hangs up
jokes.explanation: Classic Always Sunny character-based dark comedy — the joke isn't that the mom is racist, it's that Mac's correction 'They're just Muslims' treats this as perfectly reasonable while the audience knows it's not. The abrupt hang-up is a good button. The show uses the characters' awfulness as the punchline rather than endorsing the view.

dialogue.speaker: Charlie
dialogue.line: Mac, your mom burned her house down.

jokes.text: I'm very much looking forward to not taking care of anyone when I'm older.
jokes.setup: Mac is complaining about having to take care of his needy mother
jokes.punchline: Dennis volunteers that he's looking forward to not caring for anyone when old — a sociopathic inversion of normal parental concern
jokes.explanation: A wonderfully bleak Dennis line. The phrasing 'looking forward to not taking care of anyone' is specific and efficient — it captures his self-centeredness without belaboring it. Character-specific: only Dennis would frame his old age in terms of maintaining absolute freedom from obligation.

dialogue.speaker: Mac
dialogue.line: Do you have any idea what happens in those places, dude? Why don't I just rape her myself?

jokes.text: Hell, no, I'm not gonna take care of you. You were a terrible father to me.
jokes.setup: Frank says he'll get Deandra/Dee to take care of him in old age; Mac asks if Dennis won't take care of him
jokes.punchline: Dennis's flat refusal citing Frank's failures as a father — delivered without self-pity, just as a logical reason
jokes.explanation: Good character work — the flatness of Dennis's delivery is the joke. He doesn't say it with resentment or sadness, just as a matter of fact. The relationship history between Dennis and Frank adds weight to what could be a throwaway line.

dialogue.speaker: Dennis
dialogue.line: My God, I can't believe that dog's not dead. Didn't you get him when you were, like, ten?

jokes.text: You chased her out with a pool cue because she had a cough.
jokes.setup: Frank says Dee will take care of him when he's old
jokes.punchline: Dennis points out Frank already destroyed that relationship — by chasing Dee away with a pool cue for having a cough
jokes.explanation: One of the episode's best lines. The specificity is what makes it — not just 'you were mean to her' but 'you chased her out with a pool cue BECAUSE SHE HAD A COUGH.' The escalating specificity (pool cue + mundane trigger) is perfectly calibrated. It's delivered as a dry corrective, which makes it land harder. The line also retroactively explains the opening scene of Dee getting sick and Frank being dismissive.

dialogue.speaker: Charlie
dialogue.line: He ate a couple cigarette butts off the ground. He's got a wheeze. He might have emphysema, man.

jokes.text: Hey-oh! Good news, Dennis. Mom's okay.
jokes.setup: Charlie just told Mac his mom burned her house down
jokes.punchline: Mac's first reaction is to frame this catastrophic event as 'good news' — leading with what's NOT the problem
jokes.explanation: The 'good news' framing before disclosing the house fire is a good structure gag — it primes us for relief and then immediately makes the disaster worse. Mac's upbeat 'Hey-oh!' is an inspired choice of delivery for such bad news.

dialogue.speaker: Dennis
dialogue.line: Yeah, it looks like his eye is falling out.

dialogue.speaker: Mac
dialogue.line: You just pop it back with your knuckle.

jokes.text: She fell asleep with a lit cigarette in her mouth and burned the entire house down, but the good news is she's fine.
jokes.setup: Mac delivers the specifics of the house fire disaster
jokes.punchline: He buries the 'good news' at the END after describing the catastrophe — reversing the standard structure of bad news/good news delivery
jokes.explanation: The repeated 'good news' framing doubles down on the joke from the previous line. Mac's complete nonchalance about a house fire is consistent character work. The cigarette detail is appropriately on-brand for Mrs. Mac.

dialogue.speaker: Mac
dialogue.line: I'm not going to vacuum your ceiling.

jokes.text: I'll stay in a shelter.
jokes.setup: The question of where Mac's mom will stay comes up; everyone assumes she'll stay with the gang
jokes.punchline: Frank immediately offers to stay in a shelter as the obvious solution — prioritizing his own avoidance of inconvenience
jokes.explanation: Perfect Frank economy. The joke is that Frank — a wealthy man — immediately volunteers to live in a homeless shelter to avoid a minor domestic inconvenience. The delivery must be completely sincere for it to work, and in context it clearly is. This is deeply character-specific.

dialogue.speaker: Dennis
dialogue.line: They could be like The Golden Girls. You know, a couple of old ladies getting together, chasing men, eating cheesecake.

jokes.text: Nursing home? Do you have any idea what happens in those places, dude? Why don't I just rape her myself?
jokes.setup: Someone suggests a nursing home for Mrs. Mac
jokes.punchline: Mac's objection to nursing homes is rape — and his hyperbolic alternative of doing it himself is meant as dark sarcasm but lands as deranged
jokes.explanation: Shock value dark humor that leans on the show's willingness to go there rather than precise craft. The escalation from 'nursing homes are dangerous' to 'I'll do it myself' is a valid comedic logic, but the joke feels a bit cheap. It gets a laugh from the audacity rather than structure.

dialogue.speaker: Mac
dialogue.line: Oh, it popped back out.

jokes.text: Poppins! Hey, buddy! How you doing? ... I can't believe that dog's not dead.
jokes.setup: Mac's ancient, decrepit dog Poppins arrives — the name is both incongruous and reveals the dog was named when Mac was a child
jokes.punchline: Everyone's immediate reaction isn't affection but shock that the dog is still alive, implying it looks absolutely terrible
jokes.explanation: The setup is good — Mac's childhood dog named 'Poppins' introduces both sentimentality and absurdity. The payoff that everyone immediately questions how it's still alive sets up the episode's running Poppins gag. The dog visually must look horrible for this to fully land.

dialogue.speaker: Dee
dialogue.line: Josh Groban comes to town and we consider it a call to action.

dialogue.speaker: Frank
dialogue.line: What you're saying is very dorky.

jokes.text: He would disappear for months, but he would always come home. / Yeah, it looks like his eye is falling out. / You just pop it back in with your knuckle. I'll show you how to do it.
jokes.setup: Mac nostalgically describes Poppins as a survivor who always came home
jokes.punchline: Dennis observes the dog's eye is bulging out; Mac casually explains the technique for popping it back in with a knuckle as if this is normal dog ownership
jokes.explanation: The escalation from 'this dog is a survivor' to 'his eye falls out and you pop it back with your knuckle' is excellently structured. Mac's casualness about the eye-popping technique is the comedic peak — he treats it as a helpful dog-ownership tip. The image is vivid and gross in the best Always Sunny way.

dialogue.speaker: Dee
dialogue.line: No, no. I'm not doing that. Absolutely not. You're on your own.

jokes.text: It's back in, Dennis. Check it out.
jokes.setup: Dennis said he would never pop the eye back in; Mac does it anyway
jokes.punchline: Mac proudly announces he's done the gross thing and invites Dennis to verify — presumably while holding the dog up
jokes.explanation: A good button on the eye gag. Mac's pride in the accomplishment is funny, and Dennis's 'I don't care' response is the appropriate straight-man reaction. Brief and efficient.

dialogue.speaker: Frank
dialogue.line: Just make believe I'm your slave.

jokes.text: They could be like The Golden Girls. A couple of old ladies getting together, chasing men, eating cheesecake.
jokes.setup: Charlie is pitching the idea of Mac's mom and his mom living together
jokes.punchline: His Golden Girls reference reveals a sweet but completely delusional understanding of what these two difficult women are like — neither of them would ever behave like Golden Girls characters
jokes.explanation: The Golden Girls reference plants a comedic expectation that pays off brilliantly later in the episode when the two women actually bond over racism. Charlie's optimism is endearing and misguided in a way specific to his character.

dialogue.speaker: Mrs. Mac
dialogue.line: I smell like shit.

jokes.text: I'm a Grobanite. Grobanites don't miss shows. Josh Groban comes to town, and we consider it a call to action.
jokes.setup: Frank is worried Dee is too sick to go to the concert
jokes.punchline: Dee identifies herself with intense fandom vocabulary — 'Grobanite,' 'call to action' — treating a Josh Groban concert like a military obligation
jokes.explanation: Dee's pathetic obsession with Josh Groban is perfectly calibrated. The word 'Grobanite' and 'call to action' applied to a pop concert reveal her delusion. It's character-specific to Dee's desperate need to be part of something meaningful.

dialogue.speaker: Dennis
dialogue.line: Mrs. Mac has a unique and earthy fragrance.

jokes.text: What you're saying is very dorky.
jokes.setup: Dee just delivered her 'Grobanites don't miss shows' speech with great passion
jokes.punchline: Frank's flat assessment: 'very dorky' — no elaboration, no sympathy
jokes.explanation: Frank's brutal economy here is delightful. Two words that completely deflate Dee's self-importance. The flat delivery makes it land better than any elaboration would.

dialogue.speaker: Mrs. Mac
dialogue.line: Stop talking to me like I'm an asshole.

jokes.text: I got you coffee, I got you some Mexican peanuts, I got you some candy. I got you a Stud magazine.
jokes.setup: Frank is presenting a care package to Dee, ostensibly to help her feel better
jokes.punchline: The list escalates into a 'Stud magazine' — a pornographic or beefcake magazine — which is a strange gift for a sick person and reveals Frank's complete disconnect from normal caregiving
jokes.explanation: The list joke works because the first three items are almost appropriate and the fourth is completely bizarre. Frank's presentation of a pornographic magazine as standard sick-person care reveals his warped sense of comfort and bonding.

dialogue.speaker: Charlie's Mom
dialogue.line: I don't want a dog to eat my face, Charlie.

jokes.text: I'm gonna take care of you now, but when I'm old and sick, you have to take care of me. / What? No! No, I'm not doing that. Absolutely not. You're on your own.
jokes.setup: Frank reveals his entire caregiving scheme is transactional — he's explicitly trading present care for future care
jokes.punchline: Dee immediately and flatly refuses with 'You're on your own' — the transaction fails instantly
jokes.explanation: Good character work for both — Frank's transactional 'love' and Dee's immediate rejection mirror the episode's theme of nobody wanting to care for anyone. The speed of her refusal is what gives it punch.

dialogue.speaker: Frank
dialogue.line: You still get periods?

jokes.text: Frank helping Dee with something stuck in her throat — the extended physical comedy of him working on her, saying 'You okay? Yeah? No? It's down? It's going?'
jokes.setup: Dee is trying to swallow something; Frank tries to help in an intimate, uncomfortable way
jokes.punchline: The extended sequence of Frank working on Dee's throat while narrating ('It's going? Open up. Put your head back. Oh, God!') turns routine care into something deeply uncomfortable and vaguely obscene
jokes.explanation: The cringe value here comes from the uncomfortable intimacy of Frank helping Dee in this physical way. It runs a bit long for what it delivers but generates the discomfort that's the show's bread and butter. The 'Oh, God!' suggests something visually unpleasant.

dialogue.speaker: Dee
dialogue.line: Josh Groban likes his ladies to pop, so...

jokes.text: Just make believe I'm your slave. / Okay. Do my laundry.
jokes.setup: Frank offers to do anything Dee needs; she asks what that means
jokes.punchline: Frank's framing of himself as a 'slave' is immediately accepted by Dee without question — she gives an instant mundane command
jokes.explanation: Good economy — Frank's odd phrasing ('slave') and Dee's immediate, emotionless acceptance sets up the dynamic nicely. The 'do my laundry' is the right mundane command to cement her casual exploitation of him.

dialogue.speaker: Dee
dialogue.line: Josh Groban likes his ladies to pop, so...

jokes.text: I don't want to live with her. She smells. / I know she smells. / Okay, you can't talk about my mom like that!
jokes.setup: Charlie is trying to mediate the two moms meeting, acting as an 'unbiased negotiator'
jokes.punchline: His mom immediately says Mrs. Mac smells; Mac can't deny it but defends her anyway — Charlie acknowledges the smell while pretending not to
jokes.explanation: The triangle of acknowledgment/denial is well structured — Charlie's mom is blunt, Mac is defensive, Charlie tacitly confirms the smell ('I KNOW she smells') before catching himself. The truth-telling disrupts Charlie's negotiator fantasy.

dialogue.line: Dog looks like a gargoyle. He smells like piss.

jokes.text: I smell like shit.
jokes.setup: Charlie tries to diplomatically reframe Mrs. Mac's smell as a 'unique and earthy fragrance'
jokes.punchline: Mrs. Mac cuts through the euphemism with brutal self-assessment: 'I smell like shit'
jokes.explanation: Perfect economy. Four words that completely deflate Charlie's negotiator persona and reveal Mrs. Mac as someone who is under no illusions about herself. The directness is funnier than any elaborate insult could be. It's character-specific — Mrs. Mac's brand is blunt self-awareness combined with zero effort to change. Highly quotable.

dialogue.speaker: Frank
dialogue.line: As soon as you drop the soap, they rape your butt. Mac told me.

jokes.text: Stop talking to me like I'm an asshole!
jokes.setup: Charlie tries the diplomatic approach of offering Mrs. Mac perfume to 'kick off the new relationship'
jokes.punchline: Mrs. Mac sees through the condescension and objects — but her objection itself is the crude confirmation of exactly what she is
jokes.explanation: The irony that Mrs. Mac demands not to be treated like an asshole by using the word 'asshole' and being generally unpleasant is a solid self-undermining joke. Her self-awareness (she knows she's being patronized) is funnier than if she'd been oblivious.

dialogue.speaker: Dennis
dialogue.line: You need to thrust her into a hostile environment. So that she needs you to protect her.

jokes.text: Now, Mrs. Mac, I would never ask you to give up tobacco, but what if you were to switch to some sort of smokeless tobacco alternative?
jokes.setup: Charlie's mom objects to Mrs. Mac smoking in her house
jokes.punchline: Charlie's negotiated 'compromise' is to ask an elderly woman to switch from cigarettes to chewing tobacco — which is not less harmful and is arguably grosser
jokes.explanation: Charlie's 'diplomatic' solution reveals he has no idea what diplomacy means. Chewing tobacco as a 'smokeless alternative' is both logical (technically smokeless) and completely wrong in every other way. His earnestness makes it funnier.

dialogue.speaker: Dennis
dialogue.line: You need to thrust her into a hostile environment. So that she needs you to protect her.

jokes.text: I know that grunt. She's open to it.
jokes.setup: Mrs. Mac responds to the chewing tobacco suggestion with an unintelligible grunt
jokes.punchline: Mac confidently interprets this as openness — revealing a lifetime of translating his mother's inarticulate communications
jokes.explanation: One of the episode's best lines. 'I know that grunt' is an extraordinary piece of character writing — it tells us everything about Mac's relationship with his mother, the communication style of their household, and his pathetic intimacy with her dysfunction. It's deeply specific to Mac and Mrs. Mac, completely earned, economical, and deeply funny. The line could only come from this relationship.

dialogue.speaker: Frank
dialogue.line: I should dump her under the bridge.

jokes.text: That means absolutely.
jokes.setup: Mrs. Mac responds to the trial run proposal with another grunt/gesture
jokes.punchline: Mac confidently translates the ambiguous response as 'absolutely' — again acting as his mother's interpreter
jokes.explanation: A callback to 'I know that grunt' that works as a running gag. 'That means absolutely' is a good second beat. Slightly less surprising than the first but still efficient.

dialogue.speaker: Charlie's Mom
dialogue.line: I don't go to the supermarket. The shopping carts are dangerous.

jokes.text: She is terrified of animals eating her face off. / I don't want a dog to eat my face, Charlie!
jokes.setup: Mac wants to bring Poppins inside
jokes.punchline: Charlie's mom's objection to dogs is not 'I'm scared of dogs' but specifically that she fears having her face eaten — a vivid, specific, escalated fear
jokes.explanation: The specificity of 'eating her face off' vs. generic dog fear is the joke. Charlie's earnest repetition of her exact words ('She doesn't want a dog eating her face') as if it's a reasonable, reportable concern makes it funnier. This is excellent character work for Charlie's mom.

dialogue.speaker: Mac
dialogue.line: Yeah, well, she doesn't like to brag. It's not her style.

jokes.text: Laundry's done! / Those white shorts on top? That's part of my outfit for tomorrow, so why don't you go and run an iron over those?
jokes.setup: Frank announces proudly that he finished the laundry as instructed
jokes.punchline: Dee immediately assigns another task without acknowledgment — treating the completion of one task as simply the opportunity to assign the next
jokes.explanation: A solid payoff on the slave dynamic — Dee has fully leaned in and treats Frank like household staff. The escalation of tasks builds toward the eventual reversal. Functional but not outstanding.

dialogue.speaker: Dennis
dialogue.line: Yeah, there was just three people working at Jiffy Lube. It's not really a high climb.

jokes.text: Uh, you're not ragging it, are you? / You still get periods?
jokes.setup: Frank sees the white shorts and makes an observation
jokes.punchline: Frank's attempt to 'bond' involves asking Dee about her menstrual cycle — his idea of intimacy is deeply, specifically wrong
jokes.explanation: Frank's attempt at bonding through asking about periods is a perfect encapsulation of his character — he's trying but completely tone-deaf. The 'I'm trying to bond with you' explanation makes it worse in the best way. 'Ragging it' as vintage Frank slang adds texture.

dialogue.speaker: Dennis
dialogue.line: She seems like she's never been in sunlight.

jokes.text: Self-tanner, for tomorrow. Got to look good for Groban. The tan's gonna make the white in the outfit pop, the white's gonna make the tan pop. Josh Groban likes his ladies to pop.
jokes.setup: Frank asks what the cream Dee is applying is
jokes.punchline: Dee's explanation reveals an elaborate aesthetic theory constructed around what 'Josh Groban likes' — she has detailed imaginary knowledge of his preferences
jokes.explanation: Dee's pop/tan/pop logic is delusionally circular but delivered with complete confidence. 'Josh Groban likes his ladies to pop' is an excellent line — the word 'his ladies' implies an intimacy and ownership she has entirely fabricated. Good character specificity for Dee's pathetic wishful thinking.

dialogue.speaker: Charlie's Mom
dialogue.line: Charlie, she's spitting into my porcelain.

jokes.text: Dog looks like a gargoyle. / Yeah. He smells like piss.
jokes.setup: Frank brings Poppins to Dee's apartment for company while she's sick
jokes.punchline: Dee and Frank's assessments of the dog — 'gargoyle' and 'smells like piss' — are presented as normal observations about a pet
jokes.explanation: 'Gargoyle' is a good specific word choice for a visually horrifying old dog. The two characters' completely flat delivery of these descriptions as matter-of-fact observations adds to the comedy.

dialogue.speaker: Mac
dialogue.line: Look at her!

dialogue.speaker: Charlie's Mom
dialogue.line: Don't look at me.

dialogue.speaker: Mac
dialogue.line: Turn your head.

jokes.text: He ate a whole bottle of shampoo at our apartment earlier. He loves shit like that.
jokes.setup: Frank warns about keeping Poppins away from Dee's self-tanner cream because he'll eat it
jokes.punchline: Frank provides context: the dog already ate a whole bottle of shampoo, presented as endearing behavior
jokes.explanation: Seeds the later payoff when Poppins 'dies' from drinking the juice. 'He loves shit like that' as an affectionate character description of a dog that eats shampoo is a good foreshadowing joke. The rewatch bonus is for how it sets up the false death later.

dialogue.speaker: Dennis
dialogue.line: It's like Mr. Magoo.

jokes.text: Trying to score brownie points with your sister. I mean, I need somebody to take care of me when I'm old and sick.
jokes.setup: Dennis catches Frank doing Dee's bidding
jokes.punchline: Frank admits his entire caretaking scheme is nakedly transactional — no pretense of affection, just explicit future-care investment
jokes.explanation: Frank's honesty about his motives is funny but not surprising at this point in the episode. The joke works as confirmation of his character rather than revelation.

dialogue.speaker: Mac
dialogue.line: Why are you doing everything in threes?

dialogue.speaker: Charlie's Mom
dialogue.line: Oh, so Charlie doesn't die.

jokes.text: I'm not gonna put myself into one of those crypts. As soon as you drop the soap, they rape your butt. / That's what happens. Mac told me.
jokes.setup: Dennis suggests Frank check himself into a nursing home since he can afford it
jokes.punchline: Frank's objection is the dropped-soap rape myth — and his source is Mac, which explains everything
jokes.explanation: The callback to Mac's nursing home fear pays off nicely here — Mac has apparently been spreading this belief to Frank. Dennis's response ('you people have a very strange conception of what goes on in nursing homes') is the perfect straight-man button.

dialogue.speaker: Charlie
dialogue.line: I'm still alive. Can't be crazy.

jokes.text: God! You people have a very strange conception of what goes on in nursing homes.
jokes.setup: Frank reveals Mac told him nursing homes are rape factories
jokes.punchline: Dennis's exasperated, clinical response acknowledges both Mac and Frank's shared delusion
jokes.explanation: Dennis as the relatively sane voice among chaos is a reliable Always Sunny dynamic. 'You PEOPLE' implies a whole community of nursing home misconceptions, which is funnier than 'you.' Functional straight-man work.

dialogue.speaker: Mrs. Mac
dialogue.line: The Muslims are back. Damn foreigners! They ain't American, I don't want to know 'em.

jokes.text: You need to thrust her into a hostile environment so that she needs you to protect her.
jokes.setup: Frank wants to know how to make Dee need him; Dennis explains why the current approach isn't working
jokes.punchline: Dennis's advice is to deliberately create dependency through manufactured danger — delivered as strategic wisdom
jokes.explanation: Classic Dennis manipulation advice delivered as completely reasonable relationship strategy. The word 'thrust' is a small but good choice. This is Dennis at his most chillingly competent-at-being-terrible, which is a hallmark of the character.

dialogue.speaker: Mac
dialogue.line: It's not really a Golden Girls type conversation, it's, like, a racist conversation

jokes.text: I should dump her under the bridge! / Dump her under the bri- No, don't dump her down by the bridge. What are you talking about?
jokes.setup: Dennis tells Frank to put Dee in a 'hostile environment' to make her need him
jokes.punchline: Frank's interpretation of 'hostile environment' is immediately 'dump her under the bridge' — an absurd leap that reveals Frank's mind goes to literal abandonment
jokes.explanation: One of the episode's funniest beats. Frank's mind goes straight to 'dump her under the bridge' as the solution to 'hostile environment' — not a bad neighborhood, not a camping trip, but THE BRIDGE. The specificity of 'the bridge' (as if there's a specific one he has in mind) is perfect. Dennis's horrified correction ('No, don't dump her DOWN BY THE BRIDGE') is the ideal straight-man response. Highly quotable and the comedic peak of this scene.

dialogue.speaker: Dee
dialogue.line: What is going on with my face?!

dialogue.speaker: Frank
dialogue.line: It's the bedbugs.

jokes.text: If this is gonna work, then she's gonna need to feel more than just a tickle in her throat. So, if she's not feeling sick, then we're just gonna have to make her feel sick.
jokes.setup: Dennis is advising Frank on how to make Dee dependent on him
jokes.punchline: Dennis's plan escalates to deliberately making Dee sick — he delivers this as a matter-of-fact fixer's solution
jokes.explanation: Dennis diagnosing the problem and prescribing 'make her sick' as the solution reveals his psychopathy in his most competent register. The 'fixer' self-identification and 'that's what I do' is good character reinforcement.

dialogue.speaker: Dennis
dialogue.line: Oh, I think Poppins got into the juice.

dialogue.speaker: Frank
dialogue.line: He's dead?

dialogue.speaker: Dennis
dialogue.line: Yes!

dialogue.speaker: Frank
dialogue.line: He's dead!

jokes.text: You're good. / Well, I'm a fixer, Frank. That's what I do. / Dennis, listen. We should hang out more together. / Yeah. Stop trying to bond with me.
jokes.setup: Dennis has just advised Frank to deliberately make Dee sick
jokes.punchline: Frank admires Dennis's sociopathy; Dennis shuts down Frank's attempt at bonding with the same bluntness he uses on everyone
jokes.explanation: The irony that Dennis's advice to Frank was about bonding strategies while he simultaneously refuses to bond with Frank is a nice structural touch. 'Stop trying to bond with me' is a great Dennis line.

dialogue.speaker: Charlie
dialogue.line: What are you gonna do, send him to the moon?

jokes.text: They're not even talking to each other. / My mom's not very verbal.
jokes.setup: Charlie and Mac observe their two moms sitting together in complete silence
jokes.punchline: Mac's explanation — 'my mom's not very verbal' — is an enormous understatement for a woman who communicates exclusively in grunts
jokes.explanation: Perfect understatement. 'Not very verbal' as the description of a woman who may have never formed a sentence in her life is exactly the kind of thing Mac would say. Good callback to the grunt translation bits.

dialogue.speaker: Charlie
dialogue.line: He's just in here chowing down on a diaper. Hey! Look at him.

jokes.text: I know, but they haven't even touched their cheesecake. I feel like if you and I were in a room with a perfectly good cheesecake, all sorts of conversation would start happening.
jokes.setup: Charlie's Golden Girls plan isn't working — the two women sit in silence ignoring the cheesecake
jokes.punchline: Charlie's theory that cheesecake is the catalyst for female friendship/conversation is an absurd but earnest belief, and his projection of himself and Mac as a comparison is oddly sweet
jokes.explanation: Charlie's earnest belief that cheesecake is a social lubricant, and his confidence that he and Mac would talk more with cheesecake present, is a wonderfully specific absurdist take. The Golden Girls callback pays off here with gentle irony — his plan is failing in every detail except the cheesecake detail he's fixated on.

dialogue.speaker: Dennis
dialogue.line: That dog just does not die.

jokes.text: Mom, no, not me. You got to talk to HER, okay? Don't talk to me. Pretend like we're not even here.
jokes.setup: Charlie's mom starts talking to Charlie instead of Mrs. Mac
jokes.punchline: Charlie's frantic redirection reveals his plan is falling apart — his mom won't follow the script
jokes.explanation: Functional cringe comedy as Charlie's negotiator fantasy collapses. Not a standout joke but serves the scene's escalating failure arc.

dialogue.speaker: Artemis
dialogue.line: Look, if you see her biatch tell her to get her ass down here. Grobin's feeling frisky and somebody's gotta tap that ass.

jokes.text: Maybe you were at a supermarket one time, and you met a cute guy, and you were feeling saucy... So you're like Blanche, and she's like Sophia.
jokes.setup: Charlie tries to prompt conversation between the two moms with Golden Girls roleplay
jokes.punchline: Charlie assigns Mrs. Mac the role of Blanche (the sexually adventurous one) and his decrepit mother the role of Sophia — a completely tone-deaf casting
jokes.explanation: The specific casting is funny — assigning the smelly, grunt-based Mrs. Mac as Blanche reveals how far Charlie's delusion goes. 'Feeling saucy' as a prompt for a woman who may have never felt saucy is another good detail.

dialogue.speaker: Dee
dialogue.line: Grobin!!! Noooo!

jokes.text: I don't go to the supermarket. The shopping carts are dangerous. / Shopping carts are not dangerous, Mom. There's nothing dangerous about a shopping cart!
jokes.setup: Charlie tries to use a supermarket scenario to prompt Golden Girls-style conversation
jokes.punchline: His mom's objection is that shopping carts are dangerous — an irrational fear that derails the entire exercise; Charlie's exasperated denial is the button
jokes.explanation: Charlie's mom's irrational fear of shopping carts is a perfect detail — both specific and absurd. It rhymes with Mrs. Mac's fear of her face being eaten. Charlie's frustrated overreaction ('There's nothing dangerous about a shopping cart!') is appropriately disproportionate and funny.

jokes.text: I'm hot. / My mom's hot. I'm hot too. / I got to be honest. I'm hot as well.
jokes.setup: The TV has been turned off; everyone is trying to bond
jokes.punchline: The cascade of 'I'm hot too' confessions escalates the discomfort — everyone is suffering but nobody thought to address it until now
jokes.explanation: The cascading admission that everyone is hot is a mild escalation joke. Charlie's 'I got to be honest' before admitting he's hot is a small funny touch. Functional but not strong.

jokes.text: Mom was the manager at Jiffy Lube for many years. / There's only three people working at Jiffy Lube. It's not really a high climb.
jokes.setup: Charlie brags about his mom's managerial career at Jiffy Lube to find common ground
jokes.punchline: Mac immediately deflates it: Jiffy Lube has three employees, so being manager is not an achievement
jokes.explanation: 'There's only three people working at Jiffy Lube' is well-calibrated deflation. Charlie's indignation ('please don't diminish my mother's achievements') followed by Mac doubling down is a good rhythmic exchange. Mac's bluntness serves the joke.

jokes.text: Mom, do you want to take a look at that fan and see if you can fix it? [grunt] / What was that? / It means, 'Not right now, but there's a possibility that I could get to it tomorrow.'
jokes.setup: Mac tries to give his mom a task to bond with Charlie's mom; she responds with an ambiguous grunt
jokes.punchline: Mac provides an absurdly specific, diplomatic translation of what was clearly just a dismissive grunt
jokes.explanation: The best iteration of the grunt translation running gag. The specificity of 'not right now, but there's a POSSIBILITY that I could get to it tomorrow' is extraordinary — Mac has translated a grunt into a carefully hedged commitment. The escalating detail in each translation is a perfect running gag structure.

jokes.text: See, the problem is, once that sun goes down, you're not gonna get this woman to do anything, 'cause she thrives on sunlight. / She seems like she's never been in sunlight.
jokes.setup: Mac explains his mother's relationship with sunlight as a motivator
jokes.punchline: Charlie's observation that Mrs. Mac appears to have never been in sunlight contradicts Mac's claim — she's clearly not a solar-powered person
jokes.explanation: Mac's earnest belief in his mother's sunlight dependency and Charlie's flat contradiction based on visual evidence is a good two-hander. 'She seems like she's never been in sunlight' is a vivid descriptor of Mrs. Mac's presumably pallid appearance.

jokes.text: Oh! That's nasty. / Oh, Charlie, she's spitting into my porcelain.
jokes.setup: Mrs. Mac has apparently started spitting — presumably chewing tobacco
jokes.punchline: Charlie's mom's indignant complaint that Mrs. Mac is spitting into her 'porcelain' (a container she values) captures the class tension of the living arrangement
jokes.explanation: The payoff on the smokeless tobacco compromise — Mrs. Mac is now spitting into Charlie's mom's valued porcelain. The 'my porcelain' phrasing is a nice character detail for Charlie's mom's sense of dignity amid her poverty.

jokes.text: Maybe I can get you, like, a beer bottle. Would that be okay? An empty beer bottle to spit in?
jokes.setup: Charlie's mom objects to Mrs. Mac spitting in her porcelain
jokes.punchline: Charlie's diplomatic solution is to provide a beer bottle as a spittoon — the most downmarket possible resolution
jokes.explanation: Charlie's solution is on-brand — his frame of reference doesn't include spittoons or even nice containers; an empty beer bottle is his best offer. The 'would that be okay?' politeness is a good touch.

jokes.text: Mac and Charlie singing the Golden Girls theme song to the two old women who are ignoring each other, eventually getting Mrs. Mac to fall asleep
jokes.setup: Nothing else is working; Mac and Charlie desperately try to create the Golden Girls atmosphere they envisioned
jokes.punchline: Two grown men earnestly singing the Golden Girls theme in a dingy apartment to two grumpy old women — and it somehow works (Mrs. Mac falls asleep)
jokes.explanation: The payoff of the Golden Girls setup is genuinely inspired. Mac and Charlie singing 'Thank You for Being a Friend' earnestly while coaching the women on where to look is a perfect absurdist escalation that also pays off the entire setup. The fact that it WORKS (Mrs. Mac falls asleep) adds a final layer. This is the kind of comedy Always Sunny does best — commitment to a bit taken to its logical extreme.

jokes.text: You gotta stare at her. / Don't look at me! / Turn your head.
jokes.setup: Mac and Charlie are singing the Golden Girls theme and directing the two women on how to interact
jokes.punchline: Mac and Charlie's stage direction during the song — telling the old women where to look — reveals they've fully committed to producing this Golden Girls moment
jokes.explanation: The stage direction mid-song adds another comedic layer. Mac and Charlie simultaneously singing and directing is a great image — their total investment in this absurd project is what makes it funny.

jokes.text: She's zonked. When she wakes up, she'll be really, really cold, so you just give her this blanket. Give her some more juice. Just be a dad to her.
jokes.setup: Mrs. Mac has fallen asleep during the Golden Girls song.
jokes.punchline: Charlie's instructions to Frank include 'just be a dad to her' — delivered as advice to Frank on how to care for an elderly woman, completely unaware of the irony that Frank is a terrible father who doesn't know how to be a dad to anyone.
jokes.explanation: The irony of Charlie telling Frank — a notoriously bad father — to 'be a dad' is well-constructed but doesn't quite land as a punchline. It functions better as a character beat than a joke.

jokes.text: Oh, this is so boring. This is bullshit. I mean, God — how long do I have to do this for? / We've been here for, like, an hour, Frank. You're the worst dad.
jokes.setup: Frank is watching Dee sleep, fulfilling his caretaker role
jokes.punchline: Frank immediately complains about how boring it is; Mac's response 'we've been here for like an hour, you're the worst dad' is delivered with weary certainty
jokes.explanation: 'You're the worst dad' is delivered as a simple statement of fact, which is the right tone. The 'we've been here for like an hour' context makes Frank's impatience funnier — he can't even maintain a performance for 60 minutes.

jokes.text: Groban! / Ooh, she's up. / Okay. Daddy's here. Take it easy, honey. / You sing so good.
jokes.setup: Dee wakes up from a drug/medicine-induced haze, apparently dreaming about Josh Groban
jokes.punchline: Dee in her confused state thinks she's at the Groban concert; Frank tries to play along by calling himself 'Daddy' — an extremely odd choice
jokes.explanation: Dee's medicated Groban fantasy is funny; Frank's 'Daddy's here' as a soothing response is both characteristically inappropriate and oddly touching. 'You sing so good' — her complimenting an imaginary Groban — is a good detail.

jokes.text: Ooh, she's going to hit the skateboard. Ooh. / Wow. Did you see that? / She's like Mr. Magoo.
jokes.setup: Dee, in her medicated zombie state, is walking through the apartment and everyone is narrating
jokes.punchline: Dee presumably hits the skateboard and falls or stumbles; Mac compares her to Mr. Magoo — an elderly near-sighted cartoon character
jokes.explanation: Physical comedy that is better in visual form than transcript. The 'Mr. Magoo' callback is an inspired choice — it implies Dee's stumbling incompetence. The spectator narration ('she's going to hit the skateboard') is a good framing device.

jokes.text: Oh. / Magoo never made that mistake.
jokes.setup: Dee does something (falls, bumps into something) that apparently Mr. Magoo would not have done
jokes.punchline: Frank's specific defense of Mr. Magoo's competence — Dee has apparently done something WORSE than the famously incompetent cartoon — is a perfect deadpan button
jokes.explanation: One of the episode's sharpest lines. The economy is extraordinary — four words that say Dee has just done something incompetent enough that even Mr. Magoo, the benchmark of comedic incompetence, would not have done it. Frank's sincere defense of Magoo's honor elevates it further. Highly quotable, deeply specific.

jokes.text: Mrs. Kelly, why are you doing everything in threes? / Oh. So Charlie doesn't die.
jokes.setup: Mac notices Charlie's mom doing everything in counts of three; she pauses before answering with complete serenity
jokes.punchline: Her explanation — 'So Charlie doesn't die' — is delivered as matter-of-fact, as if this is an obvious and established fact
jokes.explanation: One of the episode's best jokes. The setup is perfect — a straight question about odd behavior. The punchline 'So Charlie doesn't die' is extraordinary for its simplicity, the implied OCD/magical thinking, and what it reveals about Charlie's upbringing. It deepens Charlie's character (this is WHY he is the way he is) while being hilarious. The delivery must be completely sincere for maximum effect. Exceptional character integration — this only works for Charlie's mom explaining her behavior regarding Charlie.

jokes.text: That's crazy. / Bat-shit crazy.
jokes.setup: Charlie's mom has revealed she counts in threes to prevent Charlie's death
jokes.punchline: Charlie immediately agrees that his own mother's ritual is 'bat-shit crazy' — without any apparent awareness of how this reveals his background
jokes.explanation: Charlie calling his own mother's protective ritual 'bat-shit crazy' is a solid reaction beat. The lack of self-awareness is very Charlie.

jokes.text: Hey! Get the hell - Is she waking up my mom? / No! No, Mom! My mom does not like to be woken up, Mrs. Kelly! / Just one more. One more. One, two, three. / Get out of here, goddamn it!
jokes.setup: Charlie's mom, compelled by her ritual, tries to do three counts on Mrs. Mac
jokes.punchline: Mrs. Mac wakes up furious; Charlie's mom insists on completing the three-count on a hostile, cursing woman — she can't stop mid-ritual
jokes.explanation: The payoff on the three-counting gag is excellent. Charlie's mom pursuing the ritual on a furious, cursing Mrs. Mac — unable to stop mid-count — is a great escalation. The juxtaposition of gentle ritual against Mrs. Mac's rageful 'Get out of here, goddamn it!' is well-constructed cringe comedy.

jokes.text: Now you see where I get my temper, huh?
jokes.setup: Mrs. Mac has just screamed at and physically driven out Charlie's mom
jokes.punchline: Mac is PROUD of his mother's explosive fury — using it as an explanation for his own temper, as if this is a compliment
jokes.explanation: Mac's pride in inherited bad behavior is a perfect character note. 'Now you see where I get my temper' as a boast rather than an apology is exactly the kind of self-justifying logic that makes Mac the character he is.

jokes.text: Yeah, one, two, three. One, two, three. Huh. / What are you doing? / Ah, you know, just playing it safe. She's been doing it. I'm still alive. Can't be crazy.
jokes.setup: In the aftermath of the three-counting incident, Mac has started doing it himself
jokes.punchline: Mac has adopted Charlie's mom's compulsive ritual with the logic 'she's been doing it, I'm still alive, can't be crazy'
jokes.explanation: Mac catching the three-counting 'infection' is a great escalation. His logic ('I'm still alive, can't be crazy') is exactly how Mac reasons — survivorship bias applied to magical thinking. The fact that Charlie immediately calls it 'very crazy' while still considering doing it himself is a good button.

jokes.text: It does feel good to do stuff in threes.
jokes.setup: Charlie is calling Mac crazy for three-counting
jokes.punchline: Mac's sincere observation that it 'feels good' validates the irrational compulsion — he's already converted
jokes.explanation: A quick, well-delivered button on the three-counting gag. Mac's sincere endorsement of the feeling is delivered with the confidence of someone who has discovered a great life hack. Quotable as a standalone out of context.

jokes.text: This one look off to you? One, two, three. / No, it's fine. It's fine.
jokes.setup: Charlie is trying to end the three-counting; Mac continues
jokes.punchline: Charlie, having just said he's pulling the plug on the three-counting, does it himself before bed — the compulsion has spread to him too
jokes.explanation: Charlie catching the three-counting compulsion after explicitly declaring it crazy and saying they should stop is a perfect ironic escalation. The speed with which he's converted — immediately before bed — is the right comedic timing. The ritual has now spread to both of them.

jokes.text: Hey, guys. We got some bagels and coffee. One, two, three.
jokes.setup: Morning arrives; Charlie and Mac are still in Charlie's mom's apartment
jokes.punchline: Charlie, while delivering breakfast, counts to three mid-sentence — the compulsion has fully integrated into his behavior
jokes.explanation: The morning-after beat on the three-counting gag — both Mac and Charlie have fully caught the compulsion overnight. The mid-sentence three-count during a mundane breakfast delivery is a good natural integration of the running gag.

jokes.text: Oh. The Muslims are back. / Where do you think they're coming and going from? / Damn foreigners! They ain't American, I don't want to know 'em. / I know. I wish they'd all go back to the desert.
jokes.setup: Mrs. Mac spots the neighbors through the window
jokes.punchline: The two old women bond instantly over shared racism — the Golden Girls fantasy is finally happening, just not over cheesecake
jokes.explanation: The payoff to the Golden Girls setup is subverted perfectly — they DO bond, but over xenophobia rather than cheesecake and men. It also pays off Mac's earlier phone call about Muslims. The structure is tight: Charlie set up the fantasy, it failed repeatedly, and then it happens in the worst possible way. Dark but entirely earned by the show's premise of terrible people. The double callback makes it one of the episode's structural highlights.

jokes.text: So it does seem like they're bonding, right? / Yeah. It's not really a Golden Girls-type conversation. It's, like, a racist conversation, but -
jokes.setup: Mac and Charlie observe the two women finally talking animatedly
jokes.punchline: Charlie's diplomatic acknowledgment that it's 'not really a Golden Girls-type conversation, it's like a racist conversation, but —' is a beautiful understatement and meta-commentary
jokes.explanation: One of the episode's best lines. 'It's not really a Golden Girls-type conversation. It's, like, a racist conversation, but —' perfectly captures Charlie's pathetic optimism (the 'but' implies he's still counting it as progress) alongside the horror of the situation. The economy is exceptional — the acknowledgment and the qualifier fit into one sentence. Highly quotable and a great structural payoff to the entire Golden Girls throughline.

jokes.text: Where the hell is my damn screwdriver? / I'm wiping all the germs off for you. / Quit cleaning my damn tools, and sit your ass down!
jokes.setup: Mrs. Mac is working on the fan; Charlie's mom is trying to help by wiping the tools
jokes.punchline: Mrs. Mac furiously objects to having her tools cleaned — establishing that this 'bonding' is as prickly and aggressive as everything else in their relationship
jokes.explanation: Good character work for Mrs. Mac — her abrasive version of bonding involves yelling. The fact that she's yelling about someone HELPING her is very Mrs. Mac. The 'sit your ass down' command is the kind of brusque affection these characters express.

jokes.text: We might want to even consider bringing Poppins back into this mix. It does seem to be working.
jokes.setup: The mothers are now fighting. Mac and Charlie are observing from a distance.
jokes.punchline: Mac's suggestion that adding a decrepit, smelly, possibly dying dog will improve a situation that's already on fire — delivered with analytical confidence — shows how out-of-touch their management approach has been all episode.
jokes.explanation: Setup joke for Poppins' later apparent death. The logic is broken in a funny way but not a particularly sharp joke on its own.

jokes.text: Like it? ... Ooh! Yes, I do. Please don't hit me. I have sensitive skin.
jokes.setup: Mac is showing his mom something — presumably the perfume suggested earlier.
jokes.punchline: Mrs. Mac's response to the perfume — 'yes, I do, please don't hit me' — reveals an apparently abusive domestic history, delivered so casually it functions as dark comedy.
jokes.explanation: Dark comedy gem. 'Please don't hit me. I have sensitive skin.' delivered as a casual addendum to liking a perfume implies a conditioned fear response — the perfume triggers an anxiety about violence. Very dark, very funny, very character-specific to the Mac/Mrs. Mac dynamic. 'I have sensitive skin' as a reason not to be hit is an absurd specificity.

jokes.text: Good morning, sleepyhead. / What? / Yeah, you're all tied up. It's for your own safety. / Yeah, you took a dinger down the stairs.
jokes.setup: Dee wakes up to find herself tied up
jokes.punchline: Frank's cheerful 'good morning, sleepyhead' followed by the explanation that she's tied up 'for her own safety' — which turns out to be because she fell down the stairs in her medicated state
jokes.explanation: The cheerful framing of waking someone up tied to a bed as a benevolent act is classic Frank. 'You took a dinger down the stairs' is a great colloquial way to describe what must have been a terrible fall. The gap between Frank's sunny delivery and the horror of the situation is well-calibrated.

jokes.text: Okay, I'll untie you if you promise to remember that I took care of you good. / Remember that, 'cause Frank took really good care of you, so you're gonna have to take care of him.
jokes.setup: Dee demands to be untied
jokes.punchline: Frank makes untying her conditional on her acknowledging his caretaking — the transaction is explicit and immediate
jokes.explanation: Frank's explicit bargaining while Dee is literally tied up is a good beat. The hostage negotiation framing of his caregiving arrangement is funny. 'I took care of you good' as the specific standard he wants remembered is nicely colloquial.

jokes.text: It's the bedbugs. / Oh! / But that'll last a little while, but it'll go away eventually.
jokes.setup: Dee wakes up with a rash on her face and asks what's wrong with her skin
jokes.punchline: Dennis's matter-of-fact diagnosis of bedbugs — delivered with mild reassurance that it'll go away — is treating a pest infestation as an acceptable side effect of his plan
jokes.explanation: Dennis's calm delivery of 'it's the bedbugs' is perfectly executed. The 'but that'll last a little while, but it'll go away eventually' as a reassurance is horrifying — he's clearly done something involving a bedbug infestation as part of making Dee sick. The understatement is what makes it work. Highly quotable.

jokes.text: Oh, I think Poppins got into the juice. / What? / Oh, no. / What juice? / Oh. He's ice-cold. / He's dead? Poppins is dead? / Yes! He's dead! / Why would he be dead from the juice?
jokes.setup: Everyone is dealing with the morning chaos; Frank mentions Poppins and the juice
jokes.punchline: The cascade of revelations — Poppins drank the juice, Poppins is ice-cold, Poppins is dead — escalates rapidly; Dee's question 'Why would he be dead from the juice?' implies the juice was something that could kill a dog
jokes.explanation: The apparent death of Poppins is a good fake-out escalation. Dee's 'why would he be dead from the juice' is a pointed question that implies the juice was medically compromised (part of Dennis's scheme to make her sick). The panic and speed of the revelations work well.

jokes.text: Oh, my God. Mac's gonna have a fit, dude. / I drank a lot of that juice. I remember that very clearly!
jokes.setup: Poppins has apparently been killed by the juice
jokes.punchline: Dee's horror shifts from concern about Mac to the realization that she herself drank a lot of whatever killed the dog
jokes.explanation: Dee's self-focused pivot — from Mac's grief to her own potential poisoning — is excellently timed. 'I drank a lot of that juice. I remember that very clearly!' delivered with rising panic is a great character beat. The implication that whatever Dennis did to make her sick has also killed the dog is a dark but perfect escalation.

jokes.text: I have an idea, Frank. Fixer's always got a fix. / Yeah, what? / This is gonna work. This is a good idea. Grab Poppins. Let's go. / Take the dog? / Grab the dog!
jokes.setup: Poppins is dead; Mac is going to be devastated; Dennis has a fix
jokes.punchline: Dennis's mysterious confident plan involves literally grabbing the dead dog — suggesting a scheme so dark that he won't even explain it
jokes.explanation: Dennis's confident fixer persona applied to a dead-dog crisis is funny. 'Fixer's always got a fix' as a catchphrase he seems to have for himself is a good Dennis character moment. The intrigue of what he plans to do with the corpse propels the scene forward.

jokes.text: What was in the juice? Okay, hold on. Before you go, untie me. / You stay right there, Deandra. / Just real quick, you guys. / You guys, I got Groban in the park. I got a dead dog over here. / I got Groban in the park! Untie me!
jokes.setup: Everyone is rushing out with the dead dog; Dee is still tied up
jokes.punchline: Dee's escalating competing priorities — the dead dog mystery, being untied, and Josh Groban — culminate in 'I got Groban in the park! Untie me!' as her final desperate argument
jokes.explanation: The juxtaposition of Dee's very serious problem (tied up, possibly poisoned) against her very trivial priority (Josh Groban) is perfectly Dee. The escalation of 'what was in the juice' to 'I got Groban in the park' as competing urgencies is great character comedy.

jokes.text: One, two, three. / One, two, three. / Charlie, I think you're right, dude. I feel better about this. / More in control. Yeah.
jokes.setup: Mac and Charlie are heading out the next morning to find Poppins
jokes.punchline: Both are three-counting simultaneously and bonding over the comfort it provides — the ritual has become a shared experience
jokes.explanation: A good natural continuation of the three-counting gag. Mac's sincere endorsement ('I feel better about this. More in control.') shows full adoption of the compulsion. Charlie's initial 'you're right' — when he was the one who thought it was crazy — is a good ironic reversal.

jokes.text: Hey, I was just — We were hanging out, uh, in the alley, going for some air. / What's going on? / Yeah. / What are you guys doing? / Cool. We're actually looking for Poppins. / Yeah, we're gonna bring him back over to Charlie's mom's house. / They're gonna live together.
jokes.setup: Mac and Charlie encounter Dennis and Frank in the alley; Dennis and Frank are clearly hiding something (the dead dog in a trash bag)
jokes.punchline: The awkward, over-explained non-answers ('hanging out in the alley, going for some air') while clearly acting suspicious about a specific trash can
jokes.explanation: Classic sitcom uncomfortable-secret scene structure. The over-explanation ('going for some air') is a good touch. The scene works more as setup for the trash can reveal than as a standalone joke.

jokes.text: Yeah, we're gonna bring him back over to Charlie's mom's house. They're gonna live together. ... Cool. We're actually looking for Poppins.
jokes.setup: Mac and Charlie encounter someone in the alley while carrying/hiding Poppins' body.
jokes.punchline: Mac and Charlie's cover story — that they're 'looking for Poppins' to bring to Charlie's mom's house — is delivered while presumably standing next to or carrying Poppins' body.
jokes.explanation: Setup for the trash bag reveal. The gap between their story and what they're presumably doing is funny but the joke isn't fully realized until the trash bag punchline.

jokes.text: Why are you guys acting so weird? / Yeah. / Why are you — Why are you looking at that trash can?
jokes.setup: Dennis and Frank are acting suspiciously near a specific trash can
jokes.punchline: Mac's dawning suspicion focuses on the trash can — the audience knows the dog is in it
jokes.explanation: Functional tension-building beat. Mac's focus on the trash can as the specific suspicious object creates anticipation for the reveal. Standard sitcom suspense mechanics.

jokes.text: Well, he ate a lot of cold medicine, and he croaked. / I'm sorry. / Yeah, he got into some cold medicine. Sorry. / So you threw him in the trash? / What are you gonna do, send him to the moon? / Right. I mean, come on.
jokes.setup: Mac discovers Poppins is apparently dead and in a trash bag
jokes.punchline: Dennis's defense of throwing the dog in the trash — 'What are you gonna do, send him to the moon?' — treats trashing a beloved pet as the only logical alternative to moon burial
jokes.explanation: 'What are you gonna do, send him to the moon?' is one of the episode's best lines. The logic is perfect Dennis — he has identified two options (trash or moon) and chosen the sensible one. The specific choice of 'moon' is exactly right; a lesser writer would have said 'bury him.' The moon implies a scale of absurdity that makes the trash seem reasonable by comparison. Frank's 'Right. I mean, come on.' endorsement seals it. Highly quotable.

jokes.text: No, I want to have a proper burial for him. / That seemed proper enough for Poppins, you know?
jokes.setup: Mac wants a proper burial; Dennis defends the trash bag as an appropriate send-off
jokes.punchline: Dennis arguing that a trash bag is 'proper enough for Poppins' — implying the dog's character merits no better — is both dark and character-specific
jokes.explanation: Dennis's assessment that Poppins deserves exactly what he got — a trash bag — is a good dark button. 'Proper enough for Poppins' as a phrase acknowledges some standard while arguing this meets it.

jokes.text: Oh, no. He's fine. / What? / He's fine? / Yeah, he's just in here chowing down on a diaper. / Hey! Look at him.
jokes.setup: Everyone believes Poppins is dead in the trash bag
jokes.punchline: Poppins is very much alive and eating a diaper in the trash — the 'death' was another false alarm
jokes.explanation: The reveal that Poppins is alive and eating a diaper is a perfect payoff on the indestructible-dog running gag. 'He's just in here chowing down on a diaper' is exactly the kind of gross specificity the show does well. The escalation from 'he ate shampoo' to 'he ate cold medicine and survived' to 'he's eating a diaper in a trash can' maintains the character of the dog brilliantly.

jokes.text: That dog just does not die. / No, he does not. / Wow. / Oh, there he goes. / Ah. / Don't worry, guys. He will be back. / Yeah, well, let's hope not.
jokes.setup: Poppins, alive in the trash, appears to run off again
jokes.punchline: The final Poppins beat: 'He will be back' / 'Let's hope not' — the gang's attitude toward the indestructible dog has fully shifted from affection to weariness
jokes.explanation: The final Poppins joke lands well because the relationship has evolved — from 'this dog is a survivor' to active resignation. 'Let's hope not' as the last Poppins line is a great closing note on the running gag. The 'Bon Voyage, Poppins!' button adds appropriate absurdity.

jokes.text: Bon voyage, Poppins! / Have a good trip.
jokes.setup: Poppins runs off again after surviving everything
jokes.punchline: The fond farewell — 'Bon Voyage, Poppins!' — treats the dog wandering off like a departing friend on a voyage
jokes.explanation: A charming, absurdist button on the entire Poppins storyline. The formal register of 'Bon Voyage' applied to a decrepit dog wandering into an alley is a good tonal contrast. 'Have a good trip' is the right straight follow-up.

jokes.text: Yo, Frank, it's Artemis. Have you seen Dee? I'm backstage with Groban, and the party is pumpin'. Look, if you see that 'beeyatch,' tell her to get her ass down here, 'cause Groban's feeling frisky... and somebody's gotta tap that ass. / Oh! Oh, no! / Suck you later. / No! No! Groban! No!
jokes.setup: Frank gets a voicemail while Dee is still tied up and presumably unable to get to the concert
jokes.punchline: Artemis's message reveals she is backstage with Groban, he's 'feeling frisky,' and someone else is going to 'tap that ass' — Dee's greatest dream is about to be stolen while she is literally restrained by her father
jokes.explanation: The perfect ending. Artemis's message lands every beat: 'Groban's feeling frisky' and 'somebody's gotta tap that ass' — the vague reference is both funny and devastating for Dee. 'Suck you later' as Artemis's sign-off is pure character. Dee's escalating despair ('No! No! Groban! NO!') is the right emotional close — her terrible situation converges with her pathetic obsession in one devastating payoff. It also pays off Frank's scheme (he made her sick, got her tied up, missed the concert) and Dee's 'Grobanite' identity from the opening. This is the episode's comedic peak in terms of structural payoff.

jokes.text: Oh! Oh, no! Suck you later. No! No! Groban!
jokes.setup: Dee hears Artemis's voicemail about Groban being available backstage.
jokes.punchline: Dee's anguished 'No! No! Groban!' — the culmination of her entire episode arc — combined with the still presumably tied-up and bedbug-bitten physical state she's in, is the final joke. 'Suck you later' from Frank adds a perfect grace note of indifference.
jokes.explanation: Good final beat. 'Groban!' as Dee's last word is a satisfying closing joke on her plotline. 'Suck you later' from Frank is an odd but very Frank farewell. The bathos of Dee's big Groban moment reduced to a distant scream is well-structured.

tmdb_overview: Mac's mother is left homeless after she burns down her house, which leaves Charlie and Mac with no choice but to make new living arrangements; when Dee feels under the weather, Frank tries to muster his paternal instincts to care for her.
